Thus, 8 ⊕ 4 is equal to 6.

questions.question: A man finds a wallet full of cash on the street. What should he do?
questions.solution:

questions.question: A shopkeeper increases the price of a pen by 20% and then gives a 20% discount. What is the net change in price?
questions.solution:
[IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/ca81259519cadfb2d5350673c220e419e60378e9770ad26512fc8e826a8d93f1.png] __Shortcut Trick__

Successive changes: +20% and −20%

Net change = a + b + (a × b ÷ 100)

⇒ 20 + (−20) + (20 × −20 ÷ 100)

⇒ 0 − 4

⇒ 4% decrease

**∴ The correct answer is 4% decrease.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/c76c13ba2d2ab46b47f8a931ae621dac081a0cb266b142dc23f58659fac4a466.png] **__Alternate Method__**

**Given:**

Price increased by 20%

Discount given = 20%

**Formula Used:**

New Price = Original Price × Increasing Factor × Discount Factor

 ₹100 
• +20% ₹120 
• −20% ₹96 Loss = 4% 

**Calculations:**

⇒ Let original price = ₹100

⇒ After 20% increase = 100 + 20 = ₹120

⇒ Discount = 20% of 120 = ₹24

⇒ Final price = 120 − 24 = ₹96

⇒ Net change = 100 − 96 = ₹4

⇒ Loss% = 4 × 100 ÷ 100 = 4%

**∴ The correct answer is 4% decrease.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

Successive Percentage Formula

Net Change = a + b + (a × b ÷ 100), where increases are positive and decreases are negative.

Multiplying Factor Method

20% increase = ×1.20 and 20% decrease = ×0.80. Net factor = 1.20 × 0.80 = 0.96.

Equal Increase and Decrease

An x% increase followed by an x% decrease always results in a loss of x²÷100%.

Special Case

20% increase followed by 20% decrease gives loss = 20²÷100 = 4%.

questions.question: As per the Forest (Conservation) Amendment Act, 2023, which of the following categories of land is not covered under the provisions of the Act?

options.text: Land notified as forest under the Indian Forest Act, 1927
Forest land near international borders for defence projects up to 5 hectares in LWE areas
Land recorded as forest in government records as of October 25, 1980
Land proposed for silvicultural operations in reserved forests

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Forest land near international borders for defence projects up to 5 hectares in LWE areas**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Forest (Conservation) Amendment Act, 2023**, was enacted to clarify and amend the scope of the original **Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980**. It specifies which categories of land fall under the purview of the law and which are exempted to facilitate national security and public utility.
 
• According to the **2023 Amendment**, the Act applies to land **notified as forest** under the **Indian Forest Act, 1927**, or any other law for the time being in force. This ensures that legally recognized forest tracts remain protected. *Hence, statement 1 is incorrect as this land is covered under the Act.*
 
• The Act also covers land that has been **recorded as forest** in **government records** on or after **October 25, 1980**. This provision was included to align with the **Supreme Court's** **1996** **Godavarman judgement**, which expanded the definition of forests. *Hence, statement 3 is incorrect as this land is also covered under the Act.*
 
• The **Amendment** introduced specific exemptions for **strategic projects** and **security infrastructure**. It states that the Act shall **not apply** to forest land up to **5 hectares** in **Left Wing Extremism (LWE)** affected areas as notified by the **Central Government**, intended for **public utility projects**. It also exempts strategic linear projects within **100 km** of **international borders**. ***Hence, statement 2 is the correct answer as this category of land is explicitly not covered under the provisions of the Act.***
 
• Reserved forests are the most protected category of forests under the **Indian Forest Act, 1927**, and are strictly covered under the **Forest (Conservation) Act**. While certain activities like **silvicultural operations** are not treated as "non-forest purposes," the land itself remains fully covered by the Act's regulatory framework. *Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **The Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980:** This **Act** was enacted by the **Parliament of India** to provide for the conservation of forests and for matters connected therewith. It prohibits the use of forest land for **non-forest purposes** without the prior approval of the **Central Government**.
 
• **Left Wing Extremism (LWE):** Certain districts in **India** (often referred to as the **Red Corridor**) are affected by **Naxalite-Maoist insurgency**. The **2023 Amendment** seeks to speed up **infrastructure development** (like roads and communication) in these **LWE areas** by exempting small patches of land (up to **5 hectares**) from the lengthy forest clearance process.
 
• **Indian Forest Act, 1927:** This is the colonial-era law that provides the framework for declaring **Reserved Forests**, **Protected Forests**, and **Village Forests**. The **2023 Amendment** uses this **Act** as a primary reference to define "notified" forest land.
 
• **Strategic Linear Projects:** These include **National Highways**, **Railway lines**, and **communication lines** of **national importance**. The exemption for projects within **100 km** of the **Line of Control (LoC)** or **Line of Actual Control (LAC)** is aimed at enhancing **India’s** **border security** and **defence readiness**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **T.N. Godavarman Thirumulpad Case (1996):** Before the **2023 Amendment**, the **Supreme Court of India** interpreted the **1980 Act** to apply to all areas that resembled the "dictionary meaning" of forests, regardless of ownership or notification. The **2023 Act** clarifies that it only applies to lands notified or recorded as forests after **1980**, effectively narrowing the scope back to documented forests.
 
• **Exemption Limits:** Apart from the **5 hectares** for **LWE areas**, the **Amendment** also allows for up to **10 hectares** of forest land to be used for **security-related infrastructure** and up to **0.10 hectares** alongside roads or rail lines for providing access to habitations.
 
• **Non-Forest Purpose:** The **Amendment** clarifies that **silvicultural operations**, **establishment of check-posts**, **fire lines**, **wireless communications**, and **eco-tourism facilities** included in the **Working Plan** are not considered "non-forest purposes" and thus do not require the standard diversion approval.

questions.question: Which planet in our solar system is known as the "Morning Star" and the "Evening Star"?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Venus**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Venus** is the **second planet** from the **Sun** and is the brightest natural object in Earth's night sky after the **Moon**.
 
• It is famously known as the **"Morning Star"** and the **"Evening Star"** because it is often visible shortly before **sunrise** or shortly after **sunset**. ***Hence, the statement regarding its nomenclature is correct.***
 
• **Venus** is frequently referred to as **"Earth's Twin"** due to its similar **size**, **mass**, **density**, and **bulk composition**. Its diameter is about **12,104 kilometers**, which is roughly **95%** of Earth's diameter.
 
• The planet possesses an incredibly dense atmosphere consisting of more than **96% Carbon Dioxide (CO2)**. This thick layer of gas traps heat in a runaway **greenhouse effect**, making it the **hottest planet** in the solar system with surface temperatures reaching approximately **462°C (864°F)**. ***Hence, the physical characteristics support its unique status among planets.***
 
• Unlike most other planets, **Venus** exhibits **retrograde rotation**, meaning it rotates on its axis from **east to west** (clockwise). Consequently, on **Venus**, the **Sun** would appear to rise in the west and set in the east.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Mars**: Known as the **"Red Planet"** because of the **iron oxide** (rust) prevalent on its surface. It has two small moons, **Phobos** and **Deimos**, and is home to **Olympus Mons**, the largest volcano in the entire solar system. It is the **fourth planet** from the **Sun**.
 
• **Mercury**: The **closest planet** to the **Sun** and the **smallest** in the solar system. It has the shortest orbital period, taking only **88 Earth days** to revolve around the **Sun**. It lacks a significant atmosphere, causing extreme temperature variations between day and night.
 
• **Jupiter**: The **fifth planet** from the **Sun** and the **largest** in the solar system. It is a **gas giant** primarily composed of **Hydrogen** and **Helium**. It is famous for its **Great Red Spot**, a giant storm, and has at least **95 moons**, including **Ganymede**, the largest moon in the solar system.
 
• **Planetary Classification**: The first four planets (**Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars**) are **Terrestrial Planets** or **Inner Planets**, characterized by solid, rocky surfaces. The outer four (**Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune**) are **Jovian Planets** or **Gas/Ice Giants**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Albedo**: **Venus** has a very high **albedo** of approximately **0.7**. This high reflectivity is due to its permanent cover of highly reflective clouds composed of **sulfuric acid**, which prevents **70%** of sunlight from reaching the surface but makes it shine brilliantly.
 
• **Atmospheric Pressure**: The surface pressure on **Venus** is about **92 times** that of **Earth**, which is equivalent to the pressure at a depth of nearly **1 kilometer** under **Earth's** oceans.
 
• **Orbital Characteristics**: A **sidereal day** on **Venus** (one full rotation) takes about **243 Earth days**, while its **orbital period** (one year) takes about **225 Earth days**. This means a day on **Venus** is actually longer than its year.
 
• **Exploration**: The **Venera program** by the **Soviet Union** was the first to send probes that successfully landed on the surface of **Venus** in the **1970s** and **1980s**, providing the first images of its harsh, rocky terrain.
</ul

questions.question: Which type of vegetation is primarily found in the Himalayan region of India, characterized by coniferous trees and shrubs?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Temperate forests**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Temperate forests**, often referred to as **Montane Temperate forests** in the Indian context, are the primary vegetation type in the **Himalayan region** at altitudes ranging from **1500 to 3000 meters**. These forests are prominently characterized by the presence of **coniferous trees** and various **shrubs**. *Hence, this option is correct.*
 
• The **coniferous trees** found here, such as **Pine, Deodar, Silver Fir, Spruce, and Cedar**, have evolved needle-like leaves and a conical shape to survive the cold temperatures and heavy snowfall of the **Himalayas**. *Hence, the description matches this vegetation type.*
 
• **Tropical evergreen forests** are generally found in the **Terai region** and the **foothills** of the **Himalayas** up to an elevation of **1000 meters**, where the climate is warm and humid. *Hence, this statement is incorrect.*
 
• **Tundra vegetation** occurs at much higher altitudes, typically above **3600 to 4000 meters**, where the growth of tall trees is inhibited by extreme cold; this zone is dominated by **mosses, lichens**, and very short grasses. *Hence, this statement is incorrect.*
 
• **Desert vegetation** in the **Himalayan** context is restricted to the **rain-shadow areas** of the **Trans-Himalayas**, such as **Ladakh** and **Lahaul-Spiti**, which are classified as **cold deserts** with very sparse, stunted shrubs. *Hence, this statement is incorrect.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Geographic Distribution**: These **coniferous forests** cover a vast stretch of the **Himalayan range**, passing through the states and Union Territories of **Jammu and Kashmir, Ladakh, Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Sikkim, and Arunachal Pradesh**.
 
• **Species Diversity**: In the **Western Himalayas**, the **Deodar (Cedrus deodara)** is a dominant species, prized for its durable timber. In the **Eastern Himalayas**, which receive higher **rainfall**, there is a greater variety of broad-leafed trees like **Oaks** mixed with **conifers**.
 
• **Economic Uses**: The **Chir Pine (Pinus roxburghii)** is highly valued for **timber** and for the extraction of **resin** and **turpentine**. **Silver Fir** and **Spruce** are extensively used for making **paper pulp** and **packing cases**.
 
• **Shrub Layer**: The undergrowth in these forests often consists of **Rhododendrons**, **Bamboo**, and various types of **ferns**, which thrive in the moist, cool environment of the mountain slopes.
 
• **Wildlife Habitats**: This vegetation zone is the **habitat** for unique fauna including the **Kashmir Stag (Hangul)**, **Snow Leopard** (at higher fringes), **Musk Deer**, and **Himalayan Black Bear**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Altitudinal Zonation**: The **Himalayan vegetation** shows a distinct **succession** of types based on **altitude**. It starts with **Tropical** at the base, followed by **Sub-tropical**, then **Temperate (Coniferous)**, and finally **Alpine** and **Tundra** at the highest reaches.
 
• **Climatic Influence**: The shift from **broad-leaved evergreen trees** to **needle-leaved conifers** is a direct result of the **lapse rate**, where the temperature drops by approximately **6.5 degrees Celsius** for every **1000 meters** of ascent.
 
• **Conservation**: Many areas within this **temperate belt** are protected under **National Parks** like the **Great Himalayan National Park** in **Himachal Pradesh**, which is a **UNESCO World Heritage Site** known for its biodiversity.
 
• **Soil Type**: The soils in these **coniferous forests** are generally **podzolic** and **acidic** in nature, often covered with a thick layer of **humus** formed by the slow decomposition of needles.

questions.question: What term is used for organisms that break down dead plants and animals in an ecosystem?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Decomposers**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Decomposers** are organisms that break down the **organic matter** of dead plants and animals into simpler inorganic substances. They act as nature's **recycling system** by returning essential nutrients back to the soil, water, and air.
 
• This group primarily consists of **microorganisms** like **bacteria** and **fungi**. Unlike scavengers that eat dead meat, decomposers perform **chemical breakdown** of cellular remains.
 
• They play a vital role in the **nutrient cycle** (also known as the **biogeochemical cycle**). By decomposing **dead biomass**, they release **carbon**, **nitrogen**, **phosphorus**, and **potassium**, which are then reused by **Producers**.
 
• Decomposers occupy the **final trophic level** in a food chain. Without them, the **ecosystem** would be buried under accumulated dead organic waste, and the soil would lose its **fertility**.
 
• They function by secreting **digestive enzymes** onto dead matter, which dissolves the material, allowing the decomposer to absorb the **nutrients**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Producers (Autotrophs):**
 
 
• These are organisms that can manufacture their own **food** from **inorganic sources** using **solar energy** or **chemical energy**.
 
• In terrestrial ecosystems, **green plants** are the primary producers, utilizing **chlorophyll** for **photosynthesis**. In aquatic systems, **algae** and **phytoplankton** serve this role.
 
• They represent the **first trophic level** and are the fundamental source of **energy** for all other life forms.
 
 
 
• **Consumers (Heterotrophs):**
 
 
• These organisms cannot produce their own food and must rely on eating **producers** or other **animals** for **nutrition**.
 
• They are categorized based on their diet: **Herbivores** (primary consumers like **deer**), **Carnivores** (secondary/tertiary consumers like **lions**), and **Omnivores** (like **humans** and **bears**).
 
• They facilitate the **transfer of energy** across different levels of the **food web**.
 
 
 
• **Parasites:**
 
 
• A **parasite** is an organism that lives on or inside another living organism (the **host**) and benefits by deriving **nutrients** at the host's expense.
 
• Unlike decomposers, they require a **living host**. Examples include **ticks**, **lice**, **leeches** (ectoparasites), and **tapeworms** or **Plasmodium** (endoparasites).
 
• This relationship is known as **parasitism**, where one species is harmed and the other is benefited.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Detritivores vs. Decomposers:** While both deal with dead matter, **Detritivores** (like **earthworms**, **woodlice**, and **millipedes**) physically ingest and digest **detritus**, whereas **Decomposers** (bacteria/fungi) use **extracellular digestion**.
 
• **Rate of Decomposition:** The speed at which decomposers work depends on **environmental factors**. High **temperature** and high **moisture** levels generally increase the rate of **decomposition**, while **anaerobic conditions** (lack of **oxygen**) slow it down.
 
• **Humus Formation:** The process of decomposition eventually leads to the formation of **humus**, a dark, organic substance in the **soil** that is extremely rich in **nutrients** and improves **soil structure**.
 
• **Saprotrophs:** This is another technical term often used for **Decomposers**, referring to their method of **saprophytic nutrition** (feeding on decaying matter).
</ul

questions.question: What remains constant during the melting process of a pure substance?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Temperature**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• During the melting process of a **pure substance**, the **Temperature** remains constant until the entire solid has transitioned into the liquid state. This constant temperature value is defined as the **melting point** of the substance.
 
• When heat is applied to a solid at its **melting point**, the energy is not used to increase the **average kinetic energy** of the molecules, which would normally result in a temperature rise. Instead, the energy is consumed to break the **intermolecular forces** and **chemical bonds** holding the solid lattice together.
 
• The heat absorbed by the substance during this phase change without a change in temperature is known as the **Latent Heat of Fusion**. For **water**, this value is approximately **334 Joules per gram** or **80 calories per gram** at **0 degrees Celsius**.
 
• Since **temperature** is a macroscopic measure of the **average kinetic energy** of particles, and this energy remains static during the phase transition (as the energy becomes **potential energy**), the thermometer reading does not change.
 
• The **purity** of a substance is often determined by how constant the temperature remains during melting; a **pure substance** has a **sharp melting point**, whereas a mixture melts over a **range of temperatures**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Mass**: In any physical or chemical change occurring in a closed system, the **Mass** of the substance remains constant due to the **Law of Conservation of Mass**. However, mass is a general property of matter and not a specific thermodynamic variable that characterizes the phase change of melting itself.
 
• **Volume**: Most substances experience a change in **Volume** during the melting process. Generally, substances expand upon melting (volume increases), but **water** is a notable exception; **ice** is less dense than **liquid water**, meaning the **volume decreases** when ice melts.
 
• **Pressure**: While **Pressure** is often kept constant during a laboratory experiment to measure a boiling or melting point, it is an **intensive variable** that can be manipulated externally. An increase in pressure typically raises the **melting point** of most solids, but for **water**, increasing the pressure actually lowers the melting point.
 
• **States of Matter**: Melting is one of the primary **phase transitions**. Other transitions include **freezing** (liquid to solid), **vaporization** (liquid to gas), **condensation** (gas to liquid), **sublimation** (solid to gas), and **deposition** (gas to solid).

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Thermal Equilibrium**: During the melting process, the solid phase and the liquid phase of the **pure substance** coexist in a state of **thermal equilibrium**. As long as both phases are present, the system stays at the **equilibrium temperature**.
 
• **Kinetic Theory of Matter**: According to this theory, the internal energy of a substance consists of both **kinetic energy** and **potential energy**. During melting, all added heat goes into increasing the **potential energy** associated with the arrangement of molecules, leaving the **kinetic energy** (and thus the **temperature**) unchanged.
 
• **Standard Conditions**: The **Normal Melting Point** is defined as the temperature at which a substance melts at **1 atmosphere (101.325 kPa)** of pressure. For **pure water**, this is exactly **273.15 Kelvin** or **0 degrees Celsius**.
 
• **Impact of Impurities**: The presence of a solute or impurity in a **pure substance** causes **Melting Point Depression**. This is a **colligative property**, meaning the substance will begin to melt at a **lower temperature** than its standard pure state.

questions.question: Who is eligible to receive benefits under the Pradhan Mantri Ujjwala Yojana (PMUY) scheme?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Women from BPL households**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Pradhan Mantri Ujjwala Yojana (PMUY)** was launched by Prime Minister **Narendra Modi** on **May 1, 2016**, in **Ballia, Uttar Pradesh**. The scheme was introduced with the primary aim of providing **clean cooking fuel** like **LPG** to rural and deprived households.
 
• The eligibility for this scheme is specifically restricted to **women** who are at least **18 years** of age and belong to a **Below Poverty Line (BPL)** family. This ensures women's empowerment and protects their health from the hazards of smoke.
 
• The identification of beneficiaries is done through the **Socio-Economic Caste Census (SECC) 2011** data. If a household is not covered under **SECC**, they can still be eligible if they fall under categories like **SC/ST** households or **Antyodaya Anna Yojana (AAY)**.
 
• Under the scheme, the **Central Government** provides financial assistance of **₹1600** for each **LPG connection**. This amount covers the security deposit of the cylinder, pressure regulator, booklet, and pipe.
 
• The **Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas** is the nodal ministry responsible for the implementation of this scheme across the **country**. It aims to replace traditional fuels like **firewood**, **coal**, and **cow-dung cakes** which cause severe respiratory diseases.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Ujjwala 2.0 (Phase 2):** Launched in **August 2021** from **Mahoba, Uttar Pradesh**, this version aimed to cover an additional **1 crore** beneficiaries. It simplified the application process by allowing **Self-Declaration** for **migrant workers** who do not have permanent address proof.
 
• **Expanded Coverage:** While the initial focus was strictly on **BPL** families, the scope was later expanded to include **Most Backward Classes (MBC)**, **Tea and Ex-Tea Garden tribes**, **Forest Dwellers**, and people residing in **River Islands**.
 
• **Health and Environmental Impact:** According to **WHO** reports, smoke inhaled by women using unclean fuel is equivalent to burning **400 cigarettes** in an hour. PMUY helps in reducing **Indoor Air Pollution** and contributes to **environmental conservation** by reducing deforestation.
 
• **Financial Incentives:** In **Ujjwala 2.0**, the **first refill** and a **hotplate (stove)** are provided **free of cost** to the beneficiaries, further reducing the financial burden on poor families.
 
• **Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT):** The subsidy for **LPG** refills is directly credited to the bank accounts of the beneficiaries under the **PAHAL (Pratyaksh Hanstantrit Labh)** scheme to prevent leakages and corruption.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Target Achievement:** The initial target of **5 crore** connections was achieved in **2018**, which was later revised to **8 crore** and successfully met by **September 2019**, seven months ahead of the **year** deadline.
 
• **Exclusions:** A household is ineligible if any member already possesses an **LPG connection** from any **Oil Marketing Company (OMC)** like **IOCL**, **BPCL**, or **HPCL**.
 
• **Safety Standards:** As part of the scheme, beneficiaries are provided with **safety clinics** and **education** on the safe usage of **LPG cylinders** to prevent accidental fire outbreaks in rural settings.

questions.question: Which of the following is a key feature of the Stand-Up India scheme?

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Stand-Up India scheme** was launched by the **Prime Minister** on **5 April 2016** to promote entrepreneurship at the grass-root level focusing on economic empowerment and job creation.
 
• The objective of the scheme is to facilitate bank loans between ** 10 lakh** and ** 1 crore** to at least one **Scheduled Caste (SC)** or **Scheduled Tribe (ST)** borrower and at least one **Woman** borrower per bank branch.
 
• One of the most significant features of this scheme is the provision of **Collateral-free loans**. To facilitate this, the Government of India set up the **Credit Guarantee Fund Scheme for Stand-Up India (CGSSI)**, which provides a guarantee for the loans granted by banks. ***Hence, the statement regarding collateral-free loans is correct.***
 
• The scheme is specifically designed for setting up a **Greenfield enterprise**, which refers to the first-time venture of the beneficiary in the **manufacturing**, **services**, **agri-allied activities**, or **trading sector**.
 
• Loans for **green energy projects**, **real estate development**, or **export businesses** specifically are not the defining "key features" of Stand-Up India, although such businesses may qualify if they are greenfield and owned by the target demographic. ***Hence, statements 2, 3, and 4 are incorrect in the context of being unique key features.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Eligibility Criteria:**

 
 
• The entrepreneur must be above **18 years** of **age**.
 
• The enterprise must be a **Greenfield project**.
 
• In the case of non-individual enterprises, at least **51%** of the shareholding and controlling stake should be held by either an **SC/ST** or a **Woman entrepreneur**.
 
• The borrower should not be in **default** to any bank or financial institution.
 
 
 
• **Loan Characteristics:**
 
 
• The loan is a **Composite Loan** (inclusive of term loan and working capital) between ** 10 lakh** and ** 100 lakh**.
 
• The **repayment period** for the loan is **7 years**, with a maximum **moratorium period** of **18 months**.
 
• The **Interest Rate** would be the lowest applicable rate of the bank for that category (rating), not to exceed (base rate (MCLR) + 3% + tenor premium).
 
 
 
• **Implementing Agencies:**
 
 
• The scheme is operated through all **Scheduled Commercial Banks** in **India**.
 
• The **Small Industries Development Bank of India (SIDBI)** and the **National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development (NABARD)** act as the "Stand-Up Connect Centres" to guide potential entrepreneurs.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Margin Money:** The scheme originally envisaged that the borrower would contribute **25%** of the project cost as margin money. However, in the **Union Budget 2021-22**, the margin money requirement was reduced from **25%** to **15%** of the project cost.
 
• **Handholding Support:** The scheme provides more than just credit. It offers **handholding support** through a network of agencies to help with **registration**, **skill training**, **mentoring**, and **marketing**.
 
• **Portal Services:** Entrepreneurs can access the scheme through the **Standup Mitra portal**, which provides a digital interface for application and tracking.
 
• **Recent Extensions:** The **Government of India** has extended the **Stand-Up India Scheme** up to the **year 2025** to continue fostering entrepreneurship among underserved segments of society.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT included in the domain of Psychological Well-Being?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Pollution**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Psychological Well-Being (PWB)** is a multi-dimensional concept that refers to the **internal state** of a person, including their cognitive and emotional evaluations of their life as a whole.
 
• **Sense of purpose** is a core domain of psychological well-being as it provides **meaning** and a feeling that one's life has a **direction** and **goals**. *Hence, this is a part of the domain.*
 
• **Optimism** reflects a **positive outlook** and the expectation of good outcomes in the future, which is fundamental to **resilience** and emotional stability. *Hence, this is a part of the domain.*
 
• **Pollution** is an **external environmental factor** that belongs to the study of **Environmental Science** or **Public Health**; while it can negatively affect mental health, it is not an intrinsic psychological domain. *Hence, statement 3 is the correct choice as it is NOT included in the domain.*
 
• **Feeling of accomplishment** (or Achievement) is the satisfaction derived from **reaching milestones** or succeeding in tasks, which is a key pillar in psychological frameworks like the **PERMA model**. *Hence, this is a part of the domain.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Carol Ryff’s Six-Factor Model**: Developed in **1989**, this model is one of the most scientifically validated frameworks for measuring **Psychological Well-Being**. It includes **Self-acceptance**, **Personal growth**, **Purpose in life**, **Environmental mastery**, **Autonomy**, and **Positive relations with others**.
 
• **The PERMA Model**: Introduced by **Martin Seligman** (the founder of **Positive Psychology**) in his **2011** book *Flourish*, it outlines five elements of well-being: **Positive Emotion**, **Engagement**, **Relationships**, **Meaning**, and **Accomplishment**.
 
• **Subjective Well-Being (SWB) vs. PWB**: **Subjective Well-Being** (often termed **Hedonic** well-being) focuses on **happiness** and the balance of pleasure over pain, whereas **Psychological Well-Being** (**Eudaimonic** well-being) focuses on **human potential** and living a meaningful life.
 
• **Environmental Determinants**: While **Pollution** (including **air**, **noise**, and **water** pollution) is a significant **determinant** of mental health outcomes such as **Anxiety** or **Depression**, it is classified as a **stressor** or a **contextual factor** rather than a psychological domain itself.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **World Health Organization (WHO) Definition**: The **WHO** defines health as a state of complete physical, mental, and social well-being and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity. This highlights that **Well-Being** is a proactive state.
 
• **Biological Factors**: Psychological well-being is often linked to the regulation of **neurotransmitters** such as **Serotonin**, **Dopamine**, and **Oxytocin**, which facilitate feelings of **reward**, **social bonding**, and **happiness**.
 
• **Demographic Influences**: Factors like **age** (well-being often follows a **U-shaped curve** across the lifespan), **socio-economic status**, and **cultural context** can influence how different domains like **autonomy** or **achievement** are prioritized by an individual.
 
• **Impact of Climate Change**: Modern psychological studies now recognize **Eco-anxiety**, which is the chronic fear of environmental doom caused by **Pollution** and **Climate Change**, further distinguishing the external cause from the internal psychological state.

questions.question: Which constitutional article ensures the protection of the cultural and educational rights of minorities?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Article 29**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Article 29** of the **Constitution of India** specifically deals with the **protection of interests of minorities**. It ensures that any section of the **citizens** residing in the territory of **India** having a distinct **language**, **script**, or **culture** of its own shall have the right to conserve the same. ***Hence, the option Article 29 is correct.***
 
• It serves two primary purposes: Clause (1) protects the right of a group to maintain its **cultural** and **linguistic** identity, while Clause (2) guarantees the individual right of a **citizen** not to be denied admission into **educational institutions** maintained by the **State** or receiving aid out of **State funds** on grounds only of **religion**, **race**, **caste**, **language**, or any of them.
 
• Though the heading of **Article 29** mentions "minorities," the use of the phrase "**section of citizens**" in the text indicates that the protection is available to both **minorities** as well as the **majority** community in certain contexts, as interpreted by the **Supreme Court of India**.
 
• This article is part of the **Cultural and Educational Rights** (Articles **29** and **30**) enshrined in **Part III** of the **Indian Constitution**, which are fundamental to the **secular** fabric of the **country**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Article 15**:
 
 
• This article prohibits **discrimination** by the **State** against any **citizen** on grounds only of **religion**, **race**, **caste**, **sex**, or **place of birth**.
 
• It is a facet of the **Right to Equality** (Articles **14** to **18**). It ensures equal access to **public places** like shops, restaurants, and wells. ***Hence, this statement is incorrect in the context of specific minority cultural rights.***
 
 
 
• **Article 25**:
 
 
• It provides for the **freedom of conscience** and the right to freely **profess**, **practice**, and **propagate** **religion** to all persons.
 
• This right is not absolute and is subject to **public order**, **morality**, and **health**. It also allows the **State** to regulate **economic**, **financial**, or **political** activities associated with **religious practice**. ***Hence, this statement is incorrect as it deals with religious freedom rather than specific cultural/educational rights.***
 
 
 
• **Article 32**:
 
 
• Commonly referred to as the "**Right to Constitutional Remedies**," it allows **citizens** to move the **Supreme Court** for the enforcement of **Fundamental Rights**.
 
• **Dr. B.R. Ambedkar** famously described this article as the "**Heart and Soul of the Constitution**." It empowers the **court** to issue **writs** like **Habeas Corpus**, **Mandamus**, **Prohibition**, **Quo Warranto**, and **Certiorari**. ***Hence, this statement is incorrect as it is a remedial right.***

questions.question: The Mathura school of art flourished mainly during which period?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Gupta period**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Mathura school of art** is one of the most significant schools of ancient Indian sculpture that flourished prominently during the **Kushan period** and reached its artistic zenith during the **Gupta period** (from the **4th to 6th century AD**). Hence, among the given options, the **Gupta period** is the correct answer.
 
• During the **Gupta period**, the **Mathura school** evolved from the bold and masculine styles of the earlier **Kushan** era into a more refined, elegant, and spiritual form. This era is often referred to as the **"Golden Age"** of Indian art.
 
• The primary material used by the artists of the **Mathura school** throughout its existence was **spotted red sandstone**, which was locally available in **Mathura** and surrounding regions like **Sikri**.
 
• The **Gupta** influence added a sense of **inner serenity** and **grace** to the sculptures, particularly in the depiction of the **Buddha**. The "wet drapery" style, where the clothing appears transparent and clings to the body, became a hallmark of this period.
 
• **Mathura** served as a major manufacturing hub for idols, and its products were exported to various parts of **Northern India**, including **Sarnath** and **Prayagraj**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Distinction from Gandhara School:**
 
 
• The **Gandhara school** (flourished **1st century BC to 4th century AD**) was heavily influenced by **Greco-Roman** styles and used **bluish-grey schist** or **stucco**.
 
• In contrast, the **Mathura school** was purely **indigenous** and did not exhibit foreign influence, focusing on local traditions and physical mass.
 
 
 
• **Religious Diversity:**
 
 
• The **Mathura school** was unique because it produced images for three major religions: **Buddhism**, **Jainism**, and **Hinduism**.
 
• It is credited with the first anthropomorphic (human form) representations of the **Buddha**, often shown in the **Abhaya Mudra** (gesture of fearlessness).
 
• It also created statues of **Jain Tirthankaras** and **Hindu deities** like **Shiva**, **Vishnu**, and **Surya**.
 
 
 
• **Maurya Period (322–185 BC):**
 
 
• This period is known for **court art** like the **Lion Capital of Ashoka** and **monolithic pillars**. While **Mathura** was an important city, the specific "Mathura school" of sculpture had not yet developed into its characteristic form. Hence, this option is incorrect.
 
 
 
• **Mughal Period (1526–1857):**
 
 
• The **Mughal** era focused largely on **Indo-Islamic architecture** (like the **Taj Mahal**) and **miniature paintings**. Stone sculpture of deities was not a primary feature of this period due to religious practices. Hence, this option is incorrect.
 
 
 
• **British Period (1858–1947):**
 
 
• Art during the **British Raj** was dominated by **Indo-Saracenic architecture** and **Western academic realism** in painting. The ancient schools of stone sculpture like **Mathura** were no longer active in their traditional sense. Hence, this option is incorrect.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Location:** The school was centered around **Mathura** in **Uttar Pradesh**, which was a strategic junction of trade routes.
 
• **Key Features:** The **Gupta-era Mathura** sculptures are characterized by the **halo (Prabhamandala)**, which became elaborately decorated with floral and geometric patterns, unlike the plain halos of the **Kushan** period.
 
• **Historical Impact:** The **Mathura school** laid the foundation for the **Medieval** styles of Indian sculpture, influencing the development of art across **South Asia**.
 
• **Archaeological Findings:** Thousands of fragments and statues have been recovered from sites like **Kankali Tila** (Jain) and **Katra Keshavdev** in **Mathura**, now housed in the **Mathura Museum**.

questions.question: Which musical instrument is commonly associated with Indian classical music?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Sitar**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Sitar** is a plucked stringed instrument that is synonymous with **Hindustani classical music** of **Northern India**. It is recognized globally as an icon of Indian musical heritage. ***Hence, the Sitar is the correct option.***
 
• It evolved into its current form during the **18th century** in **Mughal India**, though its precursors dates back much further. It is believed to have been influenced by the **Veena** and the Persian **Sehtar**.
 
• The instrument features a long **hollow neck** and a **gourd resonance chamber** known as a **Tumba**. It typically possesses **18 to 21 strings**, including **sympathetic strings** (Tarabdar) that vibrate to produce a distinct shimmering sound.
 
• Renowned maestros like **Pandit Ravi Shankar** and **Ustad Vilayat Khan** played a pivotal role in popularizing the **Sitar** in the **Western world** during the **1960s**, notably influencing artists like the **Beatles**.
 
• The **Sitar** is used to perform **Ragas**, which are the melodic frameworks of Indian music. The player uses a wire plectrum called a **Mizrab** on the index finger to pluck the strings.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Guitar:**

 
 
• The **Guitar** is traditionally a **Western** musical instrument. However, in the context of Indian classical music, it has been modified into the **Mohan Veena** by **Pandit Vishwa Mohan Bhatt**.
 
• Despite these adaptations, the standard acoustic or electric **Guitar** is not considered a primary traditional instrument of Indian classical systems.
 
 
 
• **Violin:**
 
 
• While the **Violin** is of **European origin**, it has been completely integrated into **Carnatic classical music** (South India) since the **19th century**.
 
• Legendary musicians like **Baluswami Dikshitar** and **Lalgudi Jayaraman** adapted its playing technique to suit Indian **Gamaka** (ornamentation). While commonly used, the **Sitar** remains the more iconic "Indian" string instrument in global general knowledge.
 
 
 
• **Piano:**
 
 
• The **Piano** is a keyboard instrument rooted in **Western Classical** and **Jazz** traditions.
 
• Due to its **tempered scale** (fixed notes), it is historically difficult to perform the continuous slides (**Meend**) essential to Indian classical music, making it rare in traditional performances.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Classification of Instruments:** In Indian musicology, instruments are classified into four categories: **Tata Vadya** (Chordophones/Strings), **Sushira Vadya** (Aerophones/Wind), **Avanaddha Vadya** (Membranophones/Drums), and **Ghana Vadya** (Idiophones/Solid). The **Sitar** belongs to the **Tata Vadya** group.
 
• **Gharanas:** The playing of the **Sitar** is divided into various **Gharanas** (schools of music) such as the **Imdadkhani Gharana** (Etawah) and the **Maihar Gharana**, each with unique stylistic features.
 
• **Construction Materials:** A traditional **Sitar** is made using **Teak wood** or **Tun wood** for the neck and bridges made of **ebony** or **camel bone**. The **Tumba** is crafted from a specially seasoned **dried gourd**.
 
• **Techniques:** The **Sitar** allows for a technique called **Meend**, where the player pulls the main melody string across the **fret** to change the pitch by as much as a **fifth interval**, mimicking the human voice.

questions.question: The art of Mathura influenced which other ancient Indian art style?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Gandhara art**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Mathura School of Art** flourished during the **1st Century AD** to the **3rd Century AD** under the patronage of the **Kushana Empire**, specifically under **King Kanishka**. It is considered a purely **indigenous style** of art that developed in **Mathura**, **Uttar Pradesh**.
 
• During the **Kushana period**, the **Mathura** and **Gandhara** schools of art co-existed and significantly influenced each other. While **Gandhara art** had strong **Greco-Roman** influences, the **Mathura school** provided the **iconographic models** and indigenous spiritual features for the depiction of the **Buddha**.
 
• The **Mathura art** style influenced **Gandhara art** in the representation of the **Buddha**'s physical form, such as the **Ushnisha** (cranial bump) and the **Urna** (mark on the forehead), which were integrated into the **Graeco-Buddhist** style.
 
• The primary material used in **Mathura art** was **Red Spotted Sandstone**, which was sourced locally. This style was not limited to **Buddhism**; it also produced images related to **Jainism** (Tirthankaras) and **Hinduism** (Vishnu, Shiva, and Surya).
 
• The **Mathura school** is credited with creating the first **anthropomorphic** (human form) representations of the **Buddha** in **India**, moving away from the purely symbolic representations (like the Bodhi tree or footprints) seen in earlier traditions like **Sanchi** and **Bharhut**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Gandhara Art:**
 
 
• Located in the **Northwest Frontier** (modern-day **Pakistan** and **Afghanistan**), this style is often called the **Graeco-Buddhist School of Art**.
 
• It utilized **Blue-grey Schist** stone and was characterized by realistic human figures with **Hellenistic** features, such as wavy hair and muscular bodies.
 
• While it absorbed **Mathura**'s spiritual iconography, it retained **Roman** artistic techniques in its drapery and facial expressions.
 
 
 
• **Mughal Art:**
 
 
• This style emerged much later, during the **16th Century** to the **18th Century**, blending **Persian**, **Indian**, and **Islamic** influences.
 
• It is primarily known for its **miniature paintings** and monumental architecture like the **Taj Mahal**. It did not have a direct contemporary relationship with **Mathura art** of the **ancient period**.
 
 
 
• **Chola Art:**
 
 
• Originating in **South India** during the **9th Century** to the **13th Century AD**, this style is famous for **Dravidian architecture** and **Bronze sculptures**.
 
• The **Nataraja** (Dancing Shiva) is the most iconic example of **Chola** craftsmanship. This style developed independently of the **Northern Mathura** influence.
 
 
 
• **Rajput Art:**
 
 
• Flourishing between the **16th and 19th Centuries** in **Rajasthan**, this style is renowned for **miniature paintings** depicting **Radha-Krishna** themes and **epic stories**.
 
• It evolved from the **Western Indian** school and **Mughal** influences, belonging to the **Medieval** rather than the **Ancient** period.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• The **Kushana Dynasty**, under **Kanishka**, served as a bridge between **India** and **Central Asia**, allowing for a unique cultural synthesis that defined the **Gandhara-Mathura** interaction.
 
• **Mathura** remained a major center for religious art for over **1,200 years**, and its stylistic elements eventually paved the way for the **Gupta Art** of the **4th Century AD**, often referred to as the **"Golden Age"** of **Indian Art**.
 
• The **Mathura Buddha** is characterized by a **smiling face**, **shaven head**, and **Abhaya Mudra** (gesture of fearlessness), whereas the **Gandhara Buddha** often appears more **meditative** and **solemn**.
</ul

questions.question: Who holds the power to dissolve the Lok Sabha prior to the completion of its tenure?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**President**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Under **Article 85(2)(b)** of the **Constitution of India**, the **President** has the power to dissolve the **Lok Sabha** (the **Lower House** of **Parliament**) even before the completion of its **five-year** term. ***Hence, the statement regarding the President is correct.***
 
• The **President** generally exercises this power on the advice of the **Council of Ministers**, headed by the **Prime Minister**. However, if the **Council of Ministers** loses the confidence of the house (the **majority**), the **President** may use **discretionary power** to dissolve the house or explore the possibility of an **alternative government**.
 
• The **Prime Minister** is the head of the **government** and can recommend the dissolution to the **President**, but the **Prime Minister** himself does not hold the constitutional authority to dissolve the house. ***Hence, the statement regarding the Prime Minister is incorrect.***
 
• The **Rajya Sabha** is the **Upper House** of the **Parliament of India** and is a **permanent body**. According to **Article 83(1)**, it is not subject to dissolution; instead, **one-third** of its members retire every **second year**. ***Hence, the statement regarding the Rajya Sabha is incorrect.***
 
• The **Speaker of Lok Sabha** is the presiding officer responsible for maintaining order and adjourning the house (**sine die** or for a specific period), but the **Speaker** does not possess the legal power to dissolve the **Parliamentary** body. ***Hence, the statement regarding the Speaker is incorrect.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Composition of Lok Sabha:** According to **Article 81**, the maximum strength of the **Lok Sabha** is fixed at **550** members (following the **104th Amendment Act, 2019**, which discontinued the nomination of **two Anglo-Indians**). Currently, it consists of members elected directly by the people of **India** on the basis of **universal adult suffrage**.
 
• **Tenure and Article 83:** The normal term of the **Lok Sabha** is **five years** from the **date** of its first meeting. However, during a **Proclamation of Emergency**, this term can be extended by **Parliament** by law for a period not exceeding **one year** at a time.
 
• **Summoning and Prorogation:** **Article 85** also empowers the **President** to **summon** each **House of Parliament** to meet at such time and place as he thinks fit, ensuring that **six months** shall not intervene between its last sitting in one session and the date appointed for its first sitting in the next session.
 
• **The Role of the Election Commission:** Once the **President** dissolves the **Lok Sabha**, the **Election Commission of India** is responsible for conducting **General Elections** to constitute a new house, typically within **six months** of dissolution.
 
• **Discretionary Powers:** In a **Hung Parliament** (where no single party or coalition has a **numerical majority**), the **President** plays a crucial role in deciding whether to dissolve the house or appoint a **Prime Minister** who can prove a majority on the **floor of the house**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Qualifications for Membership:** To become a member of the **Lok Sabha**, a person must be a citizen of **India** and at least **25 years** of age. For the **Rajya Sabha**, the minimum **age** requirement is **30 years**.
 
• **The 42nd Amendment Act (1976):** This **Act** briefly increased the tenure of the **Lok Sabha** from **five** to **six years**, but the **44th Amendment Act (1978)** restored it back to **five years**.
 
• **Difference between Adjournment and Dissolution:** **Adjournment** terminates a sitting of the **House**, which is done by the **Speaker**. **Dissolution** terminates the very life of the existing **House**, and a new **House** is constituted after **general elections**.
</ul
